newsitem.title: USA: Republican leaders promise to end federal art funds.
newsitem.headline: Republican leaders promise to end federal art funds.

text.p: House Republican leaders on Thursday vowed to eliminate funding for the National Endowment for the Arts, calling it an elitist bureaucracy that promoted obscene and blasphemous works.
Led by House Speaker Newt Gingrich and joined by several senators, conservative Republicans vowed this would be the year they finally killed the agency -- a long-sought target.

Gingrich has recently been criticised by members of his own party for seeming to equivocate on the issue and for holding a cordial meeting with actor Alec Baldwin in Washington last month to discuss arts funding.
But the Georgia Republican could find no kind words for the NEA or Hollywood actors on Thursday.

"If the people who come to lobby us (on the arts) who are famous and rich would dedicate only 1 percent of their gross income to an American endowment for the arts, they would fund a bigger system than the NEA," Gingrich said.
"This is not about money. This is about an elite group that wants the government to define what art is good, and it's explicitly wrong," he said.

Two years ago, House leaders worked out a deal with NEA opponents to allocate $99.5 million for the agency in 1996 and the same amount in 1997. Funding was to end in fiscal 1998, which begins on Oct 1.

The fact that the entire Republican leadership joined the House Conservative Action Team for the news conference seemed as much a statement about the party's internal political problems as their opposition to the NEA.
Gingrich has been criticised by conservatives who fear the House was drifting and leaders do not have an agenda. Joining hands on the NEA was a step toward mending relations.

Further, despite the united show of opposition, Ohio Representative John Boehner said he did not know if Republicans would be able to muster a 218-vote majority to axe arts funding. The Senate outlook was also unclear.

Later on Thursday, a bipartisan group of NEA supporters held their own news conference, vowing to fight any effort to kill the agency. They said the NEA provided vital seed money to support small town arts projects across the nation.
Far from being elitist, supporters said the NEA had made the arts avaible to middle- and working-class Americans across the nation.

"I am in total agreement with my colleagues who argue for smaller government," New York Republican Representative Rick Lazio said. "Faced with a smaller staff and budget, the NEA now generates more private sector funds per public dollars spent than any other agency."

Conservatives have made elimination of the NEA a test of the House leadership's commitment to reducing the size of government. They charge NEA grants are clustered in large urban areas and argue that attendance at cultural events actually increased since Congress began scaling back funding.
An NEA official dismissed the charges and said there was broad bipartisan support for the agency in Congress.
"Charges of elitism are preposterous," NEA spokeswoman Cherie Simon said. "We provide access to excellent art all over the country, rural and urban areas."
